Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

background noun

of a picture or a scene

also in the background

classical

Cic. de Or. 3.101: umbram aliquam et recessum (Lewis & Short: “somewhat of shade and background”)

recessus, recessūs m.

noun, fourth declension

background; the part of a picture that stands back

Literally a going back, a retreat, and so a recess or the inner part of a place (Lewis & Short). Cicero takes it from painting for what stands back so that the lit parts stand out. Of a person in a photograph, Latin simply says what is behind him: post eum.

Other words

  • abscēdentia, abscēdentium n. pl. — the parts of a scene painted to look further away

    present participle of abscēdō used as a noun, neuter plural · also used · classical · Vitr. 7 praef. 11: alia abscēdentia, alia prōminentia esse videantur (M-O s.v. perspective)

    Vitruvius on stage painting, beside prōminentia, the parts that seem to stand forward (the foreground). A participle, not a noun of its own.

Examples

  • habeat illa in dīcendō admīrātiō ac summa laus umbram aliquam et recessum, quō magis id, quod erit illūminātum, exstāre atque ēminēre videātur

    let admiration and the highest praise in speaking have some shade and background, so that what is lit may seem to stand out and come forward the moreCic. de Or. 3.101 (Lewis & Short)

See also picture, behind.

SourcesLewis & Short: recessus · Lewis & Short: abscedo

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
